title: A 76-year-old reads a transient negative T-wave on his own Apple Watch ECG after gym exercise; work-up finds silent three-vessel disease and he has quadruple bypass surgery (Amsterdam UMC)
summary: A 76-year-old saw a transient negative T-wave in a recording from his Apple Watch ECG app after exercise; tests showed three-vessel coronary disease, and he had four bypass grafts.
account: Koster, de Winter, Verberne, Spijkerboer and Chamuleau of Amsterdam UMC reported a case in European Heart Journal Case Reports on 30 January 2024. The event is undated, but the journal received the manuscript on 26 June 2023, so the watch recording and the surgery took place before that date. The patient was a 76-year-old asymptomatic man with a strong family history of coronary disease. He had 30 years of treated hypercholesterolemia and four years of type 2 diabetes. He exercised weekly on a cross trainer. Very infrequently and “solely out of interest”, he recorded a lead-I electrocardiogram (ECG) with his Apple Watch right afterwards. On the last recording he noticed a negative T-wave that deepened over about seven minutes and normalized after 22 minutes. He had no chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness or palpitations. He consulted a cardiologist, whose resting ECG and examination were normal. A bicycle exercise test two days later reproduced the lead-I T-wave change with ST depression up to 4 mm in V5. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) showed stenoses in all coronary arteries (CAD-RADS 4). Invasive angiography showed three-vessel disease, and a perfusion scan showed reversible ischemia in 16% of the myocardium. The heart team chose surgery, and he received four bypass grafts; recovery was uneventful. A repeat exercise ECG at 11 weeks was normal. The authors note that Apple does not recommend the watch for detecting infarction or ischemia. They note that lead I is not ideal for ischemia and that the finding requires systematic study before clinical use. In 2020 cardiologists at Magna Graecia University in Catanzaro reported that Apple Watch ECGs taken at nine body positions agreed with standard 12-lead ECGs for ST-segment changes in 100 participants. The patient in this case recorded lead I only. The paper reports no output from the ECG app's rhythm classifier. The wearer saw the abnormality on the trace, and clinicians confirmed it.
purpose: The ECG app is built to record a single-lead ECG and classify atrial fibrillation. Using the trace to spot exercise-induced ischemia is, as the authors say, not endorsed by Apple.
system: Apple Watch ECG app (single lead-I recording; its rhythm classifier is not mentioned in the report)

ratings.reason: Silent, extensive, reversible ischemia from three-vessel disease was found and treated with quadruple bypass in an asymptomatic man. The authors' learning point is that such ischemia can end in exercise-induced sudden death. The counterfactual is not established.

ai_role.statement: The watch recorded a 30-second lead-I trace at the wearer's initiative. The report gives no classification result from the app. The negative T-wave was noticed by the patient and interpreted by cardiologists, who ordered the exercise test, imaging and surgery. No machine-learning output contributed to the finding as described. The single source is an independent peer-reviewed case report. No maker material was used.

brief: In a case report published on 30 January 2024, Koster and colleagues at Amsterdam UMC describe a 76-year-old man with no symptoms. On rare occasions and out of interest, he recorded a lead-I electrocardiogram (ECG) on his Apple Watch right after exercise. In the last of these recordings he noticed a negative T-wave that deepened over about seven minutes and returned to normal after 22 minutes. A cardiologist found that his resting ECG and examination were normal, but an exercise test reproduced the change. Imaging then showed three-vessel coronary disease. He received four bypass grafts and recovered uneventfully. The authors report no result from the app's rhythm classifier.[1] The watch recorded the ECG, and the patient read it before his doctors did. Whether he would have come to harm without the recording is not established. The authors write that using the watch to document ischemic changes should be studied systematically before it enters routine clinical care.[2] In a study published on 31 August 2020, cardiologists at Magna Graecia University in Catanzaro moved an Apple Watch around the body to record nine-lead ECGs from 100 participants. They reported that these ECGs agreed with standard 12-lead ECGs in identifying ST-segment changes in patients with heart attacks.[3] This patient recorded lead I alone, so the study bears on his case only in part.

fields.summary: A 76-year-old saw a transient negative T-wave in a recording from his Apple Watch ECG app after exercise; tests showed three-vessel coronary disease, and he had four bypass grafts.
fields.account: Koster, de Winter, Verberne, Spijkerboer and Chamuleau of Amsterdam UMC reported a case in European Heart Journal Case Reports on 30 January 2024. The event is undated, but the journal received the manuscript on 26 June 2023, so the watch recording and the surgery took place before that date. The patient was a 76-year-old asymptomatic man with a strong family history of coronary disease. He had 30 years of treated hypercholesterolemia and four years of type 2 diabetes. He exercised weekly on a cross trainer. Very infrequently and “solely out of interest”, he recorded a lead-I electrocardiogram (ECG) with his Apple Watch right afterwards. On the last recording he noticed a negative T-wave that deepened over about seven minutes and normalized after 22 minutes. He had no chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness or palpitations. He consulted a cardiologist, whose resting ECG and examination were normal. A bicycle exercise test two days later reproduced the lead-I T-wave change with ST depression up to 4 mm in V5. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) showed stenoses in all coronary arteries (CAD-RADS 4). Invasive angiography showed three-vessel disease, and a perfusion scan showed reversible ischemia in 16% of the myocardium. The heart team chose surgery, and he received four bypass grafts; recovery was uneventful. A repeat exercise ECG at 11 weeks was normal. The authors note that Apple does not recommend the watch for detecting infarction or ischemia. They note that lead I is not ideal for ischemia and that the finding requires systematic study before clinical use. In 2020 cardiologists at Magna Graecia University in Catanzaro reported that Apple Watch ECGs taken at nine body positions agreed with standard 12-lead ECGs for ST-segment changes in 100 participants. The patient in this case recorded lead I only. The paper reports no output from the ECG app's rhythm classifier. The wearer saw the abnormality on the trace, and clinicians confirmed it.

value.text: Neither the finding nor its clinical interpretation was an automated diagnosis. The patient recognized the trace change and clinicians ordered further tests.
